newsitem.title: USA: Web use fuels demand for second lines - Bell.
newsitem.headline: Web use fuels demand for second lines - Bell.

text.p: Bell Atlantic Corp Chairman Ray Smith said Internet use has fueled an explosion of customers ordering second phone lines and his company expects one million customers with an added line in 1997.
In addition, the regional Bell executive said his company's goal is to hook up 50 percent of its customers with second lines in five years.

"We are going to have two cars in every garage in this country. Every one of those customers with these new lines is going to demand more speed ... and higher bandwidth" than current conventional phone service can provide, he said.
He made the comments in a speech to executives attending a two-day conference here entitled "Business and Technology in the Next Millennium" sponsored by the Wall Street Journal.

Smith pointed in particular to the growth of telecommuting services, in which customers connect work from home by connecting to central offices via computer and modem as a driving force behind demand for multiple lines.
Bell Atlantic had only a "couple hundred thousand" such customers two-and-a-half-years ago, he said.
In 1995, the company had 500,000 multi-line hook-ups in its core service area. Smith estimated that the company will have signed up 800,000 second-line accounts in 1996.
Currently, 280,000 customers in Bell Atlantic's local phone market have signed up for additional phone lines known as Integrated Services Digital Network (ISDN), he said.
These special lines provide higher speed Internet connections up to four times faster than standard phone lines.
"Sales of additional telephone lines ... (will account) for more than a million in 1997," he said.

Over the longer-term, multi-line customers are expected to account for a significant proportion of the revenue. "We're targeting to have 50 percent of our customers by the end of the year 2000" with second-line hook-ups, he said.

Smith has been a leading promoter in the phone industry of so-called higher bandwidth communications applications for residential customers such as higher speed Internet access and broadband multimedia services like video on demand.
